Let me grade this write-up carefully.

The problem: 2026 integers > 1 on a blackboard. Move: choose two integers m > 1 and n > 1 from different places, replace them with gcd(m,n) and lcm(m,n)/gcd(m,n). Continue while possible. (a) Prove that after finitely many moves, exactly one integer M > 1. (b) M doesn't depend on choices.

Field mapping:
- "answer" = explicit value of M: v_p(M) = gcd(v_p(a_1), ..., v_p(a_2026)), equivalently M = prod p^{gcd_i v_p(a_i)}. (2 correct and explicit, 1 vague or only for special boards, 0 absent/wrong)
- "reduction" = (E) elementary move description: for every prime p, move replaces p-adic valuations (x,y) with (min(x,y), |x-y|), i.e., v_p(gcd) = min(x,y) and v_p(lcm/gcd) = |x-y|, and a move never outputs two 1s (if gcd = 1 the second output is mn > 1, else the first output is gcd > 1).
- "lower_bound" = (T) termination and exactly one survivor for every play: monovariant argument plus at most one and at least one > 1.
- "upper_bound" = (I) invariance of valuation gcds, hence M independent of choices.

Now check the write-up.

Answer: The boxed formula (1) states M = prod_p p^{gcd(v_p(A_1),...,v_p(A_2026))}, with v_p(1)=0 and gcd(0,...,0)=0 conventions. Also derived v_p(M) = gcd(v_p(A_1),...,v_p(A_2026)) for every prime p. This is correct and explicit. So answer = 2.

Reduction (E): The write-up, in "Proof that the value is forced," states: v_p(gcd(m,n)) = min(a,b) and v_p(lcm/gcd) = max - min = |a-b|. Thus a move replaces (a,b) by (min(a,b), |a-b|). That's the valuation description. Also, in the termination proof: "a legal move never removes all nonunits: if g>1, its first output is g>1; if g=1, its second output is mn>1." That's the "never outputs two 1s" part. So all components of (E) are present. Reduction = 2.

Lower bound (T): Termination proof: lexicographic (P, K) with P = product, K = number of nonunits. New product P' = P/g (wait, let's verify: the two new entries have product g * (lcm/g) = lcm = mn/g^2? lcm(m,n) = mn/gcd(m,n) = mn/g. Hmm: lcm = mn/g. So product of new entries = g * lcm/g = lcm = mn/g. The old product of the pair was mn. So new board product P' = P * (mn/g)/mn = P/g. Yes, P' = P/g. Correct.)

- If g > 1: P' < P strictly.
- If g = 1: new entries are 1 and mn; P' = P; K decreases by 2 then increases by 1, so K' = K - 1. Correct.

Well-foundedness: P is a positive integer, never increases, can strictly decrease only finitely many times; while P fixed, every move decreases K (a nonnegative integer), so only finitely many moves. Correct.

At most one > 1 at terminal: any two entries > 1 form a legal pair, so a move would be possible — contradiction. Correct.

At least one > 1: a legal move never removes all nonunits (as argued above); initially all 2026 entries are > 1, so at least one nonunit remains at every stage. Correct.

So lower bound = 2. Mechanism: lexicographic monovariant (product, number of nonunits) / Euclidean descent. Name it "lexicographic (product, #nonunits) monovariant".

Upper bound (I): Invariance of G_p = gcd(e_1, ..., e_2026). The write-up shows a move replaces (a,b) with (min, |a-b|), and gcd(a,b) = gcd(a, b-a) = gcd(min, |a-b|), valid when exponents are zero ("This remains valid when one or both exponents are zero"). Also the boundary audit addresses (a,a) → (a,0), (0,b) → (0,b), (0,0) → (0,0). Then G_p invariant by associativity. Terminal board has exponents (v_p(M), 0, ..., 0), gcd = v_p(M) = c via gcd(c,0,...,0) = c. So v_p(M) = initial gcd. Hence M determined by the initial board, proving choice-independence.

Wait — one subtlety: is gcd preserved for the whole board when the two new entries could be... The pair gcd is preserved: gcd(a,b) = gcd(min, |a-b|). The full board gcd G_p = gcd of all exponents; replacing the pair (a,b) with (a', b') where gcd(a,b) = gcd(a',b'), the gcd of the whole multiset is preserved. Actually more precisely: gcd(e_1,...,e_n) = gcd(gcd(a,b), other e_i's). Since pair gcd preserved, whole gcd preserved. The write-up says "Since the gcd of the selected pair of exponents is preserved, associativity of gcd shows that G_p ... is invariant under every move." That's fine.

One check: does the pair gcd equal gcd(min, |a-b|)? If a ≤ b: gcd(a, b) = gcd(a, b - a). Yes, standard Euclidean identity, valid also when a = 0 or b = 0 (gcd(0,b) = gcd(0, b-0) = b). Correct. If a = b: (a,a) → (a, 0), gcd(a,a)=a = gcd(a,0). Correct.

So upper bound = 2. Mechanism: "invariance of per-prime gcd of valuations (Euclidean identity)".

wrong_answer_stated: false. No false lemma relied upon; indeed the write-up explicitly refutes the false "product strictly decreases" claim and uses a correct two-case argument.

Wait, one more check on the claim "the process stops" — the problem says "He continues to make moves while it is possible to do so." So the process must be shown finite; the write-up shows no infinite sequence exists, so every maximal sequence terminates. And at a terminal position exactly one > 1. Good.

Also check the answer conventions: gcd(0,...,0) = 0 means if p doesn't divide any A_i, p doesn't divide M. Fine. The formula is stated correctly and the proof derives it.

One more subtle point for (I): the invariant argument requires that the terminal board is reached (termination proved) and that the terminal board's exponent vector is (v_p(M), 0, ..., 0). Yes.

Also note the write-up is for general board of 2026 numbers but proofs are general. Fine.

Potential nitpick: In the termination proof, when g = 1, "exactly two nonunits have been replaced by one" — the new entries are 1 and mn > 1, so K decreases by 1. Correct.

Also "P is a positive integer and never increases" — indeed P' = P/g ≤ P since g ≥ 1. Correct.

So scores: answer 2, reduction 2, lower_bound 2, upper_bound 2.

Mechanisms: lower_bound_mechanism: "lexicographic monovariant (product, # nonunits)"; upper_bound_mechanism: "invariant gcd of p-adic valuations (Euclidean identity)".

wrong_answer_stated: false.
